additions.source_quote: יֵשׁ צַדִּיק שֶׁהוּא מְפֻרְסָם גָּדוֹל בִּמְדִינָה אַחַת
additions.justification: The tzaddik is the primary subject of the teaching. The equivalence 'הוּא עִנְיָן' (this is the matter of) equates the tzaddik's pattern of fame/hiddenness/influence to the Zoharic image of the spring. This is the dominant node of the package. The concept does not exist as a bechina node for Torah #132 in the dataset because no bechina edges exist for Torah #132.

additions.source_quote: מַעְיָן דְּנָפֵק מֵאֲתַר חַד, וְאָזְלִי מִתְּחוֹת לְאַרְעָא, עַד שֶׁנּוֹבֵעַ וְיוֹצֵא בְּרִחוּק בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר
additions.justification: The spring (מעיין) is the Zoharic image that the Rebbe cites as the conceptual parallel to the tzaddik. Its essential nature — flowing hidden underground, gushing forth visibly at a distant point — IS the essential nature of the tzaddik's pattern of recognition and hiddenness. This is a direct bechina: the spring IS the tzaddik from the perspective of the Zohar.

additions.source_quote: מְפֻרְסָם גָּדוֹל בִּמְדִינָה אַחַת ... וְשׁוּב בִּמְדִינָה אַחֶרֶת הוּא מְפֻרְסָם
additions.justification: The tzaddik's public fame/recognition (in the two non-adjacent countries) IS the spring's visible gushing forth (נביעה) from underground at a point far from the origin. Both phenomena share the nature of 'spiritual force made visible.' This concept — the visible phase of the tzaddik's influence — is a distinct bechina aspect of the same spring-metaphor cluster.

The tzaddik's being unrecognized and 'not considered at all' in the neighboring country IS the spring flowing underground — present but invisible to those directly above it. The hiddenness is not absence but passage. The polarity is 'good' because this is a structural feature of tzaddik-influence, not a negative condition — the underground phase is part of the positive design. The text treats the tzaddik's lack of recognition in the adjacent country not as failure but as a natural property of how spiritual force flows.

additions.source_quote: וְאַף בַּמָּקוֹם שֶׁהוֹלֵךְ תְּחוֹת אַרְעָא, הוּא מַשְׁקֶה שָׁרְשֵׁי אִילָנָא
additions.justification: The hidden influence — that the spring waters tree roots even when underground — IS the tzaddik's ongoing spiritual nourishment of those who are spiritually connected (rooted) to him even when they cannot see or recognize him. This is the key positive resolution the teaching provides: hiddenness does not mean absence of influence. The concept 'hidden influence' shares the same essential nature as the underground watering of roots. This is perhaps the most theologically rich node in the teaching — it affirms that the tzaddik's power flows continuously whether recognized or not.

additions.source_quote: עַד שֶׁנּוֹבֵעַ וְיוֹצֵא בְּרִחוּק בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר
additions.justification: The spring's visible gushing forth at a distant point (נביעה) IS the tzaddik's fame and recognition in a far country. The nevi'ah — the breaking-through-to-visibility — is the bechina counterpart of פרסום הצדיק. Both represent the moment when hidden spiritual force becomes manifest in a specific locale.

The underground flow of the spring (Aramaic: מִתְּחוֹת לְאַרְעָא) IS the tzaddik's hiddenness in the neighboring country. Both share the essential nature of 'presence that passes unseen.' This node is drawn from the Zohar's Aramaic and represents the hidden phase of the tzaddik/spring dynamic.

The watering of tree roots underground (Zohar, Aramaic: מַשְׁקֶה שָׁרְשֵׁי אִילָנָא) IS the tzaddik's hidden influence on those spiritually rooted in him. This image is drawn directly from the Zohar (Parashat Tetzeh, daf 280) and is the closing image of the teaching — the affirmation that even the hidden phase of the tzaddik's flow has life-giving effect. The 'tree roots' (שרשי אילנא) represent the spiritually receptive students/followers of the tzaddik who are nourished even when they cannot perceive or articulate the source of their nourishment.

explicit_bechina_markers_in_text: The word בְּחִינַת does NOT appear in Torah #132.
The equivalence operator used is 'הוּא עִנְיָן' (this is the matter/concept of) — functions as the bechina identity statement here.

The Zohar passage introduced with 'הוּא עִנְיָן הַכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר' establishes that the tzaddik-phenomenon and the spring-phenomenon share the same essential nature (עִנְיָן = inyan = essential matter/concept).

analysis_notes.note_on_teaching_brevity: Torah #132 is exceptionally brief (2 sentences, ~70 Hebrew words). It presents one metaphor with no elaboration, no explicit bechina/eitza structure, no good/evil mirror, and no multi-stage argument. The entire conceptual content is contained within the single tzaddik-spring equivalence and its three sub-aspects (visible appearance, underground hiddenness, underground nourishment). This contrasts sharply with longer Torahs that develop multi-package graphs.
analysis_notes.note_on_no_evil_mirror: Torah #132 contains no evil counterpart. The teaching is purely a statement of structural fact about how tzaddikim operate — their influence flows like underground water. There is no mention of the sitra achra, no opposing force, and no evil analog to the spring metaphor. This is consistent with the teaching's character as a brief phenomenological observation rather than a full-scale spiritual battle narrative.
analysis_notes.note_on_zohar_source: The Zohar passage cited (Parashat Tetzeh, daf 280) is introduced as the inyan (essential concept/matter) that explains the tzaddik phenomenon — not as proof-text but as a parallel formulation of the same idea. This confirms the bechina structure: the Zohar describes the spring because the spring IS the tzaddik, and the tzaddik IS the spring.
